tribe: Banu Malik ibn an-Najjar of al-Khazraj — Ansar of Madina
era: The One Allah Named to His Messenger ﷺ
teaser: Allah commanded the Prophet ﷺ to recite the Qur'an to one man. Ubayy heard his own name and wept.
quran_mention: «لَمْ يَكُنِ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ» — Surah al-Bayyinah (98:1), the surah Qatada reports was recited to him

layers.title: Who
layers.subtitle: White-haired, sharp-tongued, and never dyed it
layers.content:
Ubayy ibn Ka'b ibn Qays, of the Banu Malik ibn an-Najjar of al-Khazraj. His kunya was Abu al-Mundhir. His mother was Suhayla bint al-Aswad, of the same clan. His sons were at-Tufayl and Muhammad.

He was of middling height, neither tall nor short. In later life his head and beard went white and he never dyed them — several men who saw him in Madina remembered him only by that: an old man with a white head, sitting in the mosque, teaching.

He could write before Islam came, at a time when writing among the Arabs was rare. That single skill placed him among the men who wrote down the revelation for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

The reports do not sand him smooth. Zirr ibn Hubaysh said plainly that there was a quarrelsomeness in Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and once had to say to him: 'Abu al-Mundhir, be gentle with me.' He was not an easy man. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, sitting with a stranger who did not recognise the white-haired figure beside him, called him something else: 'This is the master of the Muslims, Ubayy ibn Ka'b.'
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — lineage and description; Zirr ibn Hubaysh narrated through 'Asim ibn Bahdala; 'Umar's words narrated through al-Jariri from Abu Nadra

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: One of the seventy who swore in the dark
layers.content:
Ibn Sa'd notes that on this point the sources do not disagree at all: Ubayy was present at 'Aqaba with the seventy Ansar. Every authority lists him.

That pledge is where his Islam begins, and it is worth being clear what it was. Seventy men and a couple of women from Yathrib met the Prophet ﷺ at night, in a mountain pass outside Makka, during the pilgrimage season, and undertook to shelter and defend him. They were not converting privately. They were volunteering their city for whatever came next, and what came next was war with Quraysh and the siege of their own homes.

He kept the pledge to its end. He was at Badr, at Uhud, at the Ditch and at every battle with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The Prophet ﷺ tied him in brotherhood to one of the Muhajirun, though the reports differ over which — most name Talha ibn 'Ubaydullah, while Ibn Ishaq names Sa'id ibn Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl.

And all the while he kept writing. The revelation came down and Ubayy's hand was one of the hands that caught it.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — 'Aqaba, the brotherhood reports and the disagreement between them

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: 'Allah named you for that'
layers.content:
One day the Prophet ﷺ called for him and said: 'Allah has commanded me to recite to you.'

Ubayy asked back — you can hear the disbelief in it — 'Allah named me for that?'

'Allah named you for that,' he said.

Anas ibn Malik, who narrates it, says Ubayy began to weep. Qatada adds what he was told about which surah it was: 'Lam yakun' — Surat al-Bayyinah, «لَمْ يَكُنِ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ وَالْمُشْرِكِينَ مُنفَكِّينَ حَتَّىٰ تَأْتِيَهُمُ الْبَيِّنَةُ» (98:1). A surah about clear proof arriving, recited to a man who had just been told that Allah, above the seven heavens, had specified him by name.

He did not weep because he was praised. He wept because he was known.

The Prophet ﷺ also said of him: 'The reciter of my Community is Ubayy ibn Ka'b.' And when he told the ummah where to go for the Qur'an — 'Take the Qur'an from four' — Ubayy ibn Ka'b was among the four named. He himself recited the entire Qur'an through every eight days.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Virtues of the Qur'an — 'Allah has commanded me to recite to you', narrated by Anas ibn Malik; and 'Take the Qur'an from four'
layers.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Virtues of the Qur'an; the same account with Qatada's addition in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III

layers.title: The Trial and Quality
layers.subtitle: Accused of hoarding what he knew
layers.content:
Men travelled from Iraq to sit with him and found him difficult. 'Utayy as-Sa'di said it to his face: 'We come to you from afar and we hope you will teach us. When we come to you, you make light of our business, as if we were lowly to you.'

Jundub ibn 'Abdullah told the same story from the other side. He found Ubayy in a circle in the Prophet's ﷺ mosque, thin, in two garments, looking as though he had just come off a journey. He followed him home to a shabby house. Ubayy asked where he was from. 'Iraq.' Ubayy said: 'You question me a lot.' Jundub went down on his knees, raised his hands, faced the qibla and complained aloud to Allah: we spend our money, tire our bodies, travel on our mounts seeking knowledge, and when we reach them they frown at us.

Ubayy wept. Then he made a contract with his Lord out loud: 'O Allah, if You let me live until Jumu'a, I will speak what I heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and not fear the criticism of any critic in it.'

His restraint was not stinginess — asked a hypothetical question of law he would say, 'Nephew, has this happened? Then keep it from us until it occurs.' But he heard the accusation, and he did not defend himself.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — narrated from 'Utayy ibn Damra through al-Hasan, and from Jundub ibn 'Abdullah al-Bajali through Abu 'Imran al-Jawni; the fatwa exchange narrated from Masruq

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: He did not live until Jumu'a
layers.content:
Jundub waited for Friday. On Thursday he went out and found the streets of Madina full, every road blocked with people. He asked what was happening. 'You must be a stranger.' 'Yes.' 'The master of the Muslims, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, has died.'

He never gave the speech. Years later Jundub met Abu Musa al-Ash'ari in Iraq and told him the whole story, and Abu Musa said: 'Alas. If he had lived, you could have conveyed to us what he said.'

The ummah did not lose the Qur'an with him, because he had already handed it on. Ibn Sa'd records that 'Uthman gathered twelve men of Quraysh and the Ansar to compile the text, and Ubayy ibn Ka'b was among them alongside Zayd ibn Thabit — which is why Ibn Sa'd holds it firmest that Ubayy died in 30 AH under 'Uthman, though other reports put his death in 22 AH under 'Umar. He records the disagreement rather than deciding it for us.

What he leaves is two things. A recitation that runs down to every mihrab in the world. And a warning: he waited for a better day to say what he knew, and the day did not come.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — Jundub's account; Muhammad ibn 'Umar's discussion of the conflicting dates of death; the twelve compilers narrated from Muhammad ibn Sirin

quiz.prompt: What skill did Ubayy ibn Ka'b already have before Islam, which was rare among the Arabs of his time?

options.text: He was a physician
He could write
He was a horseman
He spoke Persian

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: It is why he became one of the writers of the revelation. A skill picked up in the Jahiliyya, for ordinary reasons, turned out to be the reason he was in the room.

quiz.prompt: What did the Prophet ﷺ say to Ubayy that made him weep?

options.text: 'You will be with me in the Garden'
'Allah has commanded me to recite to you'
'You are the best of the Ansar'
'Write down what I say for those who come after'

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Virtues of the Qur'an, narrated by Anas ibn Malik
quiz.scholar_reflection: He asked, 'Allah named me for that?' and was told, 'Allah named you for that.' Being praised is one thing. Being specified by name from above the heavens is another.

quiz.prompt: Which surah is reported to have been recited to Ubayy on that occasion?

options.text: Surat al-Fatiha
Surat Ya-Sin
Surat al-Bayyinah — 'Lam yakun'
Surat al-Kahf

quiz.citation: Qatada's addition to the narration of Anas ibn Malik — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III; Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Virtues of the Qur'an
quiz.scholar_reflection: Al-Bayyinah means the clear proof. The surah opens by describing people who would not be left until clear evidence came to them. It came to Ubayy in the voice of the Prophet ﷺ, in a room, for him.

quiz.prompt: How did Ubayy respond when Jundub complained that he was withholding knowledge from those who travelled to learn?

options.text: He defended himself and sent the man away
He wept and vowed to speak publicly if he lived until Friday
He said knowledge was only for the people of Madina
He began dictating to him that night

quiz.citation: Narrated from Jundub ibn 'Abdullah al-Bajali through Abu 'Imran al-Jawni — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He had answers available: he was old, he was cautious about narrating, the visitor was pressing him. He used none of them. He accepted the complaint and bound himself in front of Allah.

quiz.prompt: What happened before the Friday on which Ubayy had promised to speak?

options.text: He was called away to Syria
'Umar forbade him from speaking
He died on the Thursday
He gave the speech early, on Wednesday

quiz.citation: Narrated from Jundub ibn 'Abdullah al-Bajali — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Jundub went out on the Thursday and found the streets impassable. The master of the Muslims had died. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari's reaction, years later, was one word: alas.

quiz.prompt: Ubayy was told that Allah had named him specifically. What would it change in you to be certain you were known by name, not just by category?

options.text: It would raise the standard I hold myself to when nobody is watching
It would be more frightening than comforting
It would settle something I have been anxious about for years
I believe it and I do not live as though I believe it

quiz.citation: Reflection on Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Virtues of the Qur'an
quiz.scholar_reflection: His first response was to check: 'Allah named me for that?' Not modesty exactly. More like a man double-checking a letter addressed to him.

quiz.prompt: The sources record that Ubayy could be quarrelsome. What do you make of a book of virtues that keeps the flaw in?

options.text: It makes the virtues believable rather than decorative
It means sanctity does not require a smooth personality
It shows the reporters cared more about accuracy than reputation
It gives me somewhere to stand, given my own temper

quiz.citation: Narrated from Zirr ibn Hubaysh — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: The same man 'Umar called the master of the Muslims is the man Zirr had to ask to be gentler. Both reports sit on the same page and neither was removed.

quiz.prompt: Asked a legal question about something that had not happened, Ubayy said: keep it from us until it occurs. Where do you sit on speculating about problems you do not have?

options.text: I rehearse future problems constantly and it exhausts me
I prefer to prepare — waiting feels like negligence
I have learned that most of what I rehearsed never arrived
It depends whether the question is mine or someone else's

quiz.citation: Narrated from Masruq through ash-Sha'bi — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: 'When it occurs, we will strive for an opinion for you.' He was not refusing to help. He was refusing to answer a question that had no one standing behind it.

quiz.prompt: He promised to say what he knew — next Friday. Is there something you have been meaning to say, on a day that has not arrived yet?

options.text: Yes, and I know exactly who it is for
Yes, and I am waiting until I am more qualified to say it
I have said the easy version and withheld the real one
No — I say things too early, which has its own cost

quiz.citation: Reflection on Jundub's account — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ubayy's delay was three days long. That was enough. Abu Musa's 'alas' is not a rebuke of Ubayy — it is grief at how little margin any of us actually has.

quiz.prompt: He recited the whole Qur'an every eight days, in an age with no printed copies and no lamps to spare. What is the honest state of your own relationship with the text?

options.text: Steady, small, and I have stopped apologising for the size of it
Intense in Ramadan and thin the rest of the year
I read it more than I understand it
It has been longer than I would like to admit

quiz.citation: Narrated from Abu al-Muhallab through Abu Qilaba — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: The same report notes Tamim ad-Dari did it in seven. They were not competing. They were reporting a rhythm, the way you would report how often you eat.
